text: In Libya and Eastern Libya, Libyans actively maintain their unique cultural identity through language, dialect, and cultural adaptations, with the goal of communicating and preserving their cultural heritage. This behavior is reciprocated by the Cretan Muslim population and other Libyans, who speak Greek with heavy Turkish influence and share similar cultural adaptations. The Libyans in Eastern Libya, particularly those in Benghazi, exhibit a distinct dialect and a blend of Greek, Turkish, and Arabic influences, forging a closer connection with the Cretan Muslim population than with Afghans. This cultural exchange and preservation of identity are widely regarded as normative among the sampled population, reflecting the significance of maintaining cultural distinctiveness and historical ties within the Libyan cultural group.

In Libya, both during Gaddafi's presidency and after the revolution, people exhibit varying perceptions of safety, with a notable preference for the security experienced during Gaddafi's era. This preference reflects the cultural tendency to value perceived security, which was more prevalent under Gaddafi's rule. The sampled population appears to be divided in their views regarding the levels of safety experienced during these different periods. This behavior is considered a topic of significant debate and holds a balanced level of normativity within the sampled population, with no clear consensus on the preferred era in terms of safety.

Most Libyan people would not be categorized as being direct communicators . Many a re not very comfortable with saying NO to the requests of people whom they are not so close to because they think this answer might hurt their feelings. As they get closer in their relationships they become more comfortable with saying what they really mean or have in mind. When communicating and interacting, a person's honor and reputation are of utmost importance. Loyalty to one's family tends to takes precedence over personal needs. Social class and family background are the major determinants of personal status, followed by individual character and achievement. Libyans may openly discuss money and even ask what someone what they paid for things or what their salary is. A Libyan may openly ask why one is not married as it is considered t unusual for an adult to be unmarried and have no children. It’s best to not speak about family disagreements or any difficulty you may have had in your life. This is especially the case during initial meetings. Questions that may be considered too personal include those related to women in a family. It is best not to ask about a person's wife, sister or adult daughter. Just refer to the family as a whole. One way to avoid disclosing information that you may feel is too personal is by responding with a reference to the subject in general. For example, answering "why are you not married” by saying “ah, marriage is a wonderful thing.” This indirect approach should let your Libyan counterpart know that there is no interest in pursuing this line of conversation. They may employ similar tactics.

Public displays of affection are not acceptable and are mostly forbidden. Kissing or hugging between members of the opposite gender is not acceptable in public, even if they are married. Libyans tend to feel comfortable standing a little less than an arms length apart from one another. This space is much, much greater between men and women. There is a decent amount of touching between members of the same gender during conversations. It is common for two men to walk hand in hand in public. This does not have any implication on their sexual preferences; it's just a sign of friendship and closeness. It also very common for female friends to link arms while walking or talking. There is no touching between men and women in public places except if they are related and even then it is usually kept to a minimum.

Direct eye contact is acceptable between men and between women. Indirect eye contact with genders is often considered disrespectful. This may not be the case when interacting with superior or certain elders. Indirect to no eye contact is best between genders, especially between strangers and in public situations.

When it comes to time, Libyans tend to be relaxed about the timing of events, especially in social situations. In business situations, punctuality is desirable and appointments are usually necessary. Note that most Muslims pray five times a day: at dawn (4:30-5:00 a.m.), around noon, in the afternoon between 2:00 and 4:00, at sunset, and one hour after sunset (never later than 9:00 p.m.). Prayer times vary according to the time of year and the part of the country you may be in. At prayer time, everything stops. So if you are in a store, you would have to go outside and wait for approximately 10 to 15 minutes. It’s best to plan your schedule around prayer times.

By law, Libyan women have the same rights as men, but in practice it is not always so. While women have the rights to get promotions or to have the same opportunity to apply and get the same jobs as men, salaries are usually lower and most people still defer to men in most situations. Women cannot usually speak their minds as openly much as men, especially in public. When it comes to dress, women have to dress appropriately (mostly covered) at all times while men can dress as they please. It is rare for women to gather together at a restaurant or café. This is not usually the case for foreign women.

Keeping your hands in your pockets while in conversation with someone is usually seen as a lack of respect. If you admire something, like a work of art at a Libyan home, your host may insist that it be taken as a gift. It is considered rude to refuse this offer so be aware of how you compliment things. When eating always use the right hand as the left hand is not used and considered unclean. This is especially the case when taking food from communal dishes. Always pass and receive goods with your right hand. Touching the thumb with the tips of the fingers is a common way of adding emphasis to a point during conversation. It’s considered common behavior to stand when new guests arrive at a social gathering or when a high-ranking person enters or leaves. Men almost always stand when a woman enters the room. Don’t point the toe or heel or any part of the foot at any person. Don’t show the sole of your foot or use the foot to move anything as it is viewed as the lowliest body part. Tight or revealing clothing baring shoulders, calves, things, etc., is considered extremely rude and can lead to trouble. Disrespecting ones family name is the ultimate form of rudeness.

Alcohol is strictly prohibited. Drinking is illegal for all ages. However, there are still many underground alcohol sellers and buyers. There are also certain sanctioned hotels and clubs where drinking is allowed for foreigners. Penalties for the import, manufacture, possession, and consumption of alcohol or illegal drugs are severe. Convicted offenders can expect jail sentences, fines, public flogging, and/or deportation.

Most people are expected to dress conservatively and properly. Furthermore, some jobs require formal dress while others less so. While most Libyans appreciate business suits, they do not expect a foreigner to wear one unless in marketing positions or in a position dealing constantly with managers/Directors/CEO of Libyan companies. If you are a woman, wearing other things than long dresses/pants and long sleeves blouses would be inappropriate.
When dealing with a superior or in formal meeting, one should use Mr. or Mrs. in front of the first or last name. If there is a friendship relation, the family name or the first name is enough.

- 아랍인에 대한 정의에는 여러 의견이 있지만, 보통 아랍어를 모국어로 사용하고 아랍 문화와 이슬람교를 신봉하면 아랍인이라 함. 카다피 시대 20 리비아 개황 인 1 이슬람 도래 이전의 리비아 : 고대(8세기 이전) 리비아는 마그레브 문화권과 나일-메소포타미아의 비옥한 초승달 지역 문화권 사이에 위치해 있으나, 가혹한 기후 조건(사막) 때문에 인구가 희박하여 사실상 상기 두 문화권을 지리적으로 구분해 주는 완충 지대로 존재 - 고대 이집트 제19왕조(B.C. 가족 제도 아랍족이 643년 리비아를 정복한 후 9~10세기에 걸쳐 아라비아 반도로부터 대거 진출하여, 원주민인 베르베르족보다 다수 민족이 됨. 아랍인은 유목민 전통을 따라 부족공동체가 지니고 있는 고유의 혈연적 연대 의식과 신 앞에서 만인이 평등하다는 교우적 연대 의식을 생활기반으로 삼고 있음.

혈연을 신성시하고 혈연에 대한 충성이 생활과 사고에 크게 작용 하여 누구나 가계(家系)에 대한 자부심이 있고, 가계에 대한 비방은 용서할 수 없는 모욕으로 여기며, 이슬람의 영향으로 부족 구성원 간 에는 남녀 차별 없이 모두가 평등 오늘날 대부분의 아랍인은 부족 생활에서 벗어나 가족 중심으로 생활하며, 석유 개발과 함께 카다피 정권의 사회주의 정책으로 생활 교육 수준 향상에 따라 개인주의가 확산되면서 핵가족 제도로 점차 변모하고 있는 중 개인은 가족을 떠나서 존재할 수 없으므로 개인의 혼인 문제는 가족 전체의 문제이고, 결혼 상대는 가족 구성원이 공동으로 물색하고 서로 상의하여 택함.
전통적 아랍 관습에 따르면 이혼할 수 있는 권리는 남자에게만 있었으나 1973년 법으로 여자에게도 남자와 같이 이혼할 권리 인정 - 증 인 앞에서 “나는 너와 이혼한다”고 3회 반복 선언함으로써 이혼 성립 - 이 혼한 남자는 외국인 여자와 결혼할 수 없으며, 외국인과 결혼한 남자는 정부기관 및 정부 소속 기관에 취업하기 어려움.

의식주 생활  세계관 622년 이슬람교 탄생 이래 1,400여 년간 아랍인의 생활과 그들의 의식 구조는 이슬람 교리에서 비롯되고 있으며, ‘신의 존재를 의식 하고 신에 대한 의무를 이행하는 마음의 상태’를 말하는 타끄와 (Taqwa : fear of God)가 삶에 있어 인간적 가치를 부여하는 것이라고 인식 77 사회 및 문화  의복 남 자들은 전통적으로 흰색 면셔츠와 면바지를 입고 겨울에는 양털로 만든 외투를 착용하며, 여자들은 넓은 천으로 몸을 휘감는데 이를 바라칸(Barracan)이라 부름. 투아레그족 남자들은 푸른 물감을 들인 베일을 쓰나, 여자는 쓰지 않음.

문화 환경 카다피 철권통치 시절에 반체제 반정부 움직임을 사전 차단하기 위해 문화예술 활동을 철저히 감시 통제한 영향이 여전히 남아 있고, 내전 이후 혼란으로 문화예술 활동은 미약 향후 국내 정세 안정과 경제회복이 이루어진다면 국민 의식의 변화와 함께 이 분야도 긍정적인 변화가 있을 것으로 기대 Ⅵ 우리나라와의 관계 1. 협정 체결 현황 1977.12. 의료협력에 관한 의사록 서명 1981. 8.16. 양국 공동위 설립, 경제 과학 기술 협력 추진 양해각서 교환 1999. 9. 6. 경제 과학 기술협정 서명 1999. 9. 6. 문화협정 서명(미발효) 2001. 4. 경제 과학 기술협정 발효 2006. 9.21. 무역협정 서명 2006. 9.21. 투자증진 및 보호협정 서명 2007. 2. 무역협정 발효 2007. 3. 투자증진 및 보호협정 발효 ※ 2009.8.
